name: SolarWinds
desc: A well-known supply chain attack against an Austin, TX software company.

acts.d: Attackers embedded their malicious payload on a legitimate component of the SolarWinds Orion Platform software. This component is a DLL library, SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll

To bypass application control technologies, adversaries sign their malware with valid signatures by creating, acquiring, or stealing code-signing materials. The attackers compromised the SolarWinds digital certificates, allowing them to run privileged actions and maintain a low profile
The malicious DLL file was distributed to victims through an automated update mechanism

During the SolarWinds installation or update to victim machines, the tampered DLL is loaded by legitimate executables and installed as a Windows service. The malicious code calls the function that contains the backdoor capabilities
Once loaded, the backdoor runs a series of checks to ensure it is running in an actual environment. The backdoor also checks that the last write-time of the malicious DLL was 12-14 days ago
The backdoor checks for a variety of antivirus/endpoint detection agents prior to execution (e.g. Windbg, Autoruns, Wireshark)
The backdoor conducts basic reconnaissance on the compromised system to determine running processes to report to the C2 server.

The attacker obtains the MachineGuid registry value. This value is used to dynamically generate a portion of the C2 domain, along with the physical address of the interface and the domain name of the device
Adversaries use DGAs to dynamically generate a C2 domain rather than relying on static IP addresses

The C2 responds with an encoded buffer of commands for the backdoor to execute. The commands allow the attackers to run, stop, enumerate processes; read, write, enumerate files and registry keys; collect and upload information about the device; and restart the device

The attackers used a legitimate hostname found within the victim's environment as the hostname on their C2 infrastructure to avoid detection. The malware also masquerades its C2 traffic as the Orion Improvement Program (OIP) Protocol

The executing process creates two files on disk. 1) A VBScript typically named after existing services or folders to avoid detection. 2) The second-stage TEARDROP Cobalt Strike loader written into a legitimate-looking subfolder %WinDir%
Attackers used NETSH to configure firewall rules that limit certain UDP outbound packets before intense reconnaissance with NSLOOKUP and ADFIND
Attackers executed ADFIND to enumerate domains and to discover trust between federated accounts with a renamed filename chosen to blend into the environment
The attackers renamed Windows admin tools to conduct reconnaissance to avoid detection
Attackers used WMI to discover processes, services, and signed-in users on remote systems
The attackers created a IFEO Debugger registry value for dllhost.exe to trigger execution of the installation of Cobalt Strike
Attackers obtained Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Active Directory Service Principal Names (SPNs) to crack offline
Attackers attempted to access Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) passwords with account credentials already compromised
Attackers executed a DCSync attack in which they leveraged privileged accounts to access credentials
The TEARDROP malware is run through rundll32.exe, which runs as a service in the background to estabish persistence
The VBScript removes the previously created registry value to clean up any traces of execution and deletes two more registry keys in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\.DEFAULT

Attackers used the service control manager on a remote system to disable security monitoring processes before moving laterally. After they completed their lateral movement, they reenabled the services to avoid detection
PowerShell remote task creation enabling lateral movement
The attackers used valid accounts to move laterally
During lateral movement, custom-loader DLLs, including TEARDROP, were deployed into exiting Windows sub-directories. The files resemble legitimate Windows file and directory names
When executed during lateral movement, rundll32 ran through WMIC. The Cobalt Strike beacon was loaded onto the machine
According to Microsoft, the Cobalt Strike DLL was likely deleted after execution to avoid forensic discovery
Attackers used AUDITPOL to disable event logging while carrying out their attacks and reenabling it afterwards
Attackers used fsutil to check available free space before executing collection or exfiltration, which might create large files on disk
The attackers were able to collect sensitive data from victims
The attackers used the 7-zip utility to create a password-protected archive with an extension not associated with archive files
The attackers mapped a OneDrive share from the command-line using the net.exe command-line utility. They also likely used other cloud services such as Google Drive
